title: Gondhal: Marathi Folk Thriller Selected as India's Oscar Entry for 2027
excerpt: The Film Federation of India has chosen Santosh Davakhar's Marathi thriller Gondhal — selected from 33 submissions — as India's official entry for the 99th Academy Awards' Best International Feature Film category.
body:
• The Film Federation of India has selected Santosh Davakhar's Marathi thriller Gondhal as India's official entry for the 99th Academy Awards, announced September 18, 2026.
  • The film was chosen from 33 submissions and will compete in the Best International Feature Film category at the Oscars on March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles.
  • It is only the fourth Marathi film ever selected as India's Oscar entry, after Shwaas (2005), Harishchandrachi Factory (2009) and Court (2015).
  • Gondhal has been fully visually dubbed into seven languages — including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and English — a world-first technique that will carry it far beyond its Marathi audience.

India's Oscar pick is a Marathi folk thriller

Marathi cinema is headed back to the Academy Awards. The Film Federation of India (FFI) announced on September 18 that Gondhal, writer-director Santosh Davakhar's thriller rooted in Maharashtra's traditional Gondhal ritual, will represent India in the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards, scheduled for March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles.

The selection, announced by jury chair P. Sheshadri at a Mumbai press conference, came from a field of 33 submissions spanning Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Gujarati, Tamil, Malayalam and Nagamese, plus a silent film. Among the contenders it beat were some of the year's biggest commercial titles: Aditya Dhar's blockbuster Dhurandhar and its sequel, the devotional drama Hanuman Ansh, Border 2 and 120 Bahadur. The 14-member jury included Vijay Patkar, Tannishtha Chatterjee, Sabu Joseph and Vivek Vaswani, and deliberated over ten days, according to reports.

What the film is about

Gondhal takes its title and setting from the centuries-old Gondhal folk-performance tradition of Maharashtra — a ritual form built around music, dance and mythology. Set in rural Maharashtra and unfolding over a single high-stakes night, the film follows Suman, a married woman whose life takes an unexpected turn as relationships, desire and deception collide. What begins as a story of everyday relationships tightens into a psychological thriller, with the sacred ritual at the center of a calculated game of strategy.

The film stars Ishita Deshmukh as Suman alongside Kishor Kadam, Yogesh Sohoni, Nishad Bhoir, Anuj Prabhu, Suresh Vishwakarma and Vitthal Kale. Veteran composer Ilaiyaraaja scored the film, with Amalendu Chaudhary as cinematographer and Ashish Mhatre as editor. Released in theatres in November 2025, the roughly two-hour film had already built festival momentum: Davakhar won the Silver Peacock for Best Director at the 56th International Film Festival of India, and the film earned FIPRESCI honors from the International Federation of Film Critics at the Bengaluru International Film Festival.

"We were confident while making and submitting the film."

— Santosh Davakhar, director of Gondhal, on the Oscar selection

Why the jury picked it — and why the dubbing matters

Jury chair Sheshadri praised the film's handling of tradition, form and narrative precision, telling reporters it was "a happy moment for Indian cinema, for Marathi cinema." The selection continues a quiet Marathi tradition at the Oscars: Shwaas (2005), Harishchandrachi Factory (2009) and Court (2015) were the previous Marathi entries, making Gondhal the fourth.

What sets this entry apart is distribution. Earlier this year, Davakhar's team completed what trade press described as a world first: the film was fully visually dubbed — not just voice-dubbed, but with visuals adapted — into seven languages: Marathi, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and English. For an Oscar entry, that is strategically significant. India's submissions have historically struggled for visibility beyond their home language; a Marathi film arriving in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and English versions can build the kind of multi-language audience and press attention that Academy campaigns run on.

The diaspora angle

For Indian audiences abroad, the Academy's international feature race is often the first real window into regional cinema — and most Marathi Oscar entries have been nearly impossible to find with subtitles outside India. Gondhal's seven-language versions change that equation, giving diaspora viewers in the US, UK and the Gulf a genuine chance to watch India's official pick before the ceremony. If the film makes the Academy shortlist, expect a US theatrical or streaming push to follow.

What's next

Selection as India's entry is only the first stage. Gondhal now enters the Academy's International Feature Film process, which narrows the field to a shortlist before final nominations. The campaign window between now and March 2027 will determine whether a small Marathi thriller can do what no Indian film has done in the category's history — and with dubbed versions ready in six additional languages, its makers have given it the widest possible stage to try.
